title: How Do Viewers Synthesize Conflicting Information from Data Visualizations?
research_question: How do people combine sequentially presented, potentially conflicting graphical evidence, and how are their synthesized judgments affected by the direction, magnitude, context, and presentation order of the evidence?
methodology: The authors conducted four experiments with 1,166 participants who sequentially viewed pairs of line charts and then produced a synthesized estimate of the relationship represented by the charts. Experiment 1 used context-free variables, Experiments 2A and 2B introduced real-world contextual scenarios, and Experiment 3 added accompanying article-like text. Chart-pair slope direction, magnitude, discrepancy, and order were manipulated, while synthesis was measured through a line-drawing widget and additional numerical and decision questions. The study also collected free-text explanations and analyzed them using inductive thematic coding.

key_findings.finding: Across experiments, when both line-chart slopes pointed in the same direction, participants placed greater weight on the weaker, less steep relationship.
key_findings.section: Experiments 1-3, Direction of the presented stimuli

key_findings.finding: When the two slopes pointed in opposite directions, participants consistently weighted the positive relationship more strongly than the negative relationship.
key_findings.section: Experiments 1-3, Direction of the presented stimuli

key_findings.finding: As disagreement between the two slopes increased, synthesized judgments tended to move away from their arithmetic average and toward the stronger slope.
key_findings.section: Experiments 1-3, Discrepancy between the presented stimuli

key_findings.finding: The authors found no significant effect of whether the stronger slope was presented first or second in Experiment 1, Experiments 2A and 2B, or Experiment 3.

Different elicitation methods were generally consistent but not identical; some statistically significant differences appeared between line-drawing and text-box responses, showing that measured synthesis can depend on response modality.

The experiments provide evidence about human synthesis of two sequential conflicting information sources, but they do not test longitudinal workplace briefing, persistent work-item state, omission, repeated alerts, or false-alert decisions.

limitations: Participants synthesized only two pieces of information at a time rather than long, evolving multi-source streams.
The stimuli were restricted primarily to similar line-chart designs, limiting generalization to other visualization and document forms.
The experiments did not vary the number of underlying data points or sample sizes across the evidence sources.
Several scenarios were fictional or controlled for experimental purposes and may not reproduce real professional decision contexts.
The task studied synthesis of relationships, not tracking persistent obligations or work-item lifecycle states.
No repeated briefing cycles were generated, so omission, repetition, and false-alert rates were not jointly evaluated.
The authors caution that the study is an initial examination and is insufficient for firm design prescriptions.
raw_claims: Four experiments involved a combined 1,166 participants.
Each participant synthesized evidence from two line charts shown sequentially.
The experiments varied whether the two slopes agreed or opposed each other in direction.
Same-direction evidence was generally synthesized with more weight on the weaker slope.
Opposite-direction evidence was generally synthesized with more weight on the positive slope.
Larger discrepancies shifted synthesized estimates toward the stronger slope.
No significant presentation-order effect was detected in the reported experiments.
The authors triangulated synthesis using graphical, numerical, and decision responses.
Qualitative responses were coded to characterize participants' synthesis strategies.
Experimental stimuli, analysis materials, and data are linked through the paper's supplementary OSF resource.
